01

Chipathon 2026 · Layout Review · GF180MCU

longtin — an antenna‑free 4×2 SRAM DLA

dla_engine_top, the "tiny" INT8 GAN matrix‑multiply accelerator, hardened on a rectangular 1600 × 1100 µm die. The C result buffer is flip‑flops, so only eight SRAM macros remain — clustered into a compact central 4×2 block, which (with a density sweep) drives antennas to literal zero. Single‑supply 3.3 V, third‑party AS 3.3 V standard cells, foundry OCD SRAM IP.

Antenna 0 / 0 DRC 0 · LVS match 8 SRAM macros (4A + 4B) C buffer = flip‑flops 1.76 mm² · 57.1% util 25 MHz 121 mW

Two design moves. (1) The 24‑bit×16‑word C buffer moved from a folded 64×8 SRAM macro to ~408 flip‑flops (USE_SRAM(0)) — removing the 9th macro. (2) The eight A/B macros were clustered into a central block with 55 µm channels; a short density sweep then landed a placement that routes every net clean. Antenna went 4 → 2 → 0 with DRC/LVS/timing untouched (see slide 7).

Final routed die — 1600 × 1100 µm, clustered 4×2

The layout, two ways

Floorplan at a glance

  • A buffer (weights, row broadcast) → bottom row, 4 macros
  • B buffer (inputs, column broadcast) → top row, 4 macros
  • C buffer (results) → flip‑flops in the fabric — no macro
  • Clustered central block (55 µm channels) + perimeter logic/fill

05

Rubric 2 · Power, Ground & Current Paths

Power delivery network

IR‑drop — OpenROAD PDNSim static analysis (nom_tt)

MetricValueMeaning
Worst VDD drop0.348 mVworst cell sees 3.29965 V instead of 3.300
Worst VSS bounce0.798 mVground rail rises at most this much
Average drop0.006 mV5.8 µV — essentially nothing
Power‑grid violations0 / 0VDD / VSS — grid fully connected

Caveats: static analysis on the flow's estimated 121 mW (117 internal + 4 switching); core‑level, so this is the on‑die grid only — package/pad delivery is a padring‑stage concern. Worst droop ≈ 0.8 mV of 3.3 V (~0.02%), negligible against the +15 ns setup margin.

  • Single 3.3 V domain (VDD/VSS) — no domain crossings, no level shifting. Running VDD/VSS as closely‑spaced interleaved straps is intentional: it lowers PDN loop inductance and adds decoupling capacitance.
  • Both SRAM banks tied to the grid explicitly on Metal3 via PDN_MACRO_CONNECTIONS; well/substrate taps in every AS std cell + macro (DRC‑enforced spacing).
  • IR‑drop & EM low: 121 mW at 25 MHz with min‑drive cells; straps sized far above demand. No core ring by design — added at the padring stage.
06

Rubric 3–5 (+ 1) · Analog · Reliability · Integration

Remaining review criteria

3 Analog / Matching

Fully digital — no analog circuitry. No PLL, no matched pairs, no sensitive nodes. The only analog‑adjacent structures are the SRAM sense amps, pre‑qualified foundry IP used as‑is.

4 Reliability & PD Risk

  • Antenna: 0 violations — closed to literal zero (slide 7); no residual charge‑accumulation risk.
  • Latch‑up: taps in every std cell + macro, DRC‑enforced spacing.
  • Voltage: single 3.3 V, all AS cells + OCD SRAM 3.3 V‑rated.
  • EM / current density: negligible at 25 MHz, min‑drive cells.
  • ESD: pad‑level clamps — padring scope, out of this core block.

5 Top‑Level Integration

  • Top cell dla_engine_top everywhere (RTL ⟷ netlist ⟷ layout).
  • Pin names match RTL 1:1 — proven end‑to‑end by LVS.
  • Ports on the core boundary; ~16 µm margin ready for the shuttle padring.
  • Stage‑1 core macro; the shared padframe is a separate Stage‑2 run.

Rubric 1 recap (DRC/LVS): Magic DRC 0, routing DRC 0, GDS XOR 0; Netgen LVS matches uniquely across 23,540 devices — layout corresponds to the RTL device‑for‑device. Full signoff on slide 2.

07

Rubric 5 · Connectivity — ports vs pins

Pin requirements

A port is a named signal; a bus becomes one physical pin per bit. So the 13 ports of dla_engine_top expand to 55 pins on the die edge (what the layout shows). The packaged chip needs far fewer — a serial bridge trades those 55 for a 4‑wire link.

Core dla_engine_top — 13 ports → 55 pins

PortBitsDir
clk, rst_n, start1 eain
wr_en, wr_sel1 eain
wr_addr10in
wr_data8in
rd_en1in
rd_addr4in
rd_data24out
wb_done, done, busy1 eaout
total55+ VDD/VSS via grid

Bonded chip (+ serial bridge) — ~9 pins

PadRole
SCLK, MOSI,
CS_N, MISO		4‑wire serial link — carries all 55 bits
busy, done, wb_donestatus, wired straight out (scope‑visible)
clk, rst_ndedicated clock / reset pads
VDD, VSSpower (slot: 4 DVDD + 4 DVSS)
total9 digital pins + power

Why the bridge: the shuttle slot has only 20 general‑purpose digital pads — you can't bond out 55. dla_serial_bridge.v collapses the parallel bus onto SCLK/MOSI/CS_N/MISO, so the die's 55 pins stay on‑chip and the part talks to a host over 4 wires. This layout is the Stage‑1 core (all 55 pins on its edge); the bridge + padring are a separate Stage‑2 wrapper.

08

Reliability deep‑dive · how antennas reached zero

Antenna closure: 4 → 2 → 0

The first roomy floorplan left 4 marginal antenna nets — long SRAM→PE broadcast wires, a side‑effect of spreading the macros across a big die. Closure was a two‑lever, evidence‑driven chase:

ExperimentAntennaNote
baseline (roomy, d56)4worst 1.44×
+ diode margin 404no help — length problem
cluster 35 µm—CTS crash (too tight)
cluster 55 µm, d482macro‑broadcast net fixed
cluster + density 441
cluster + density 500 ✅winner
cluster + density 522

Lesson: extra diodes can't shorten a wire — clustering the macros shortened the broadcast nets (root cause), and a density re‑roll then routed the last marginal nets clean. All runs stayed DRC/LVS‑clean throughout.

09

Functional verification — the intended design

UVM environment (pyuvm on cocotb)

UVM (IEEE 1800.2) builds a testbench from cooperating components that speak in transactions, not wires. Here it runs in Python via pyuvm (a faithful port of the standard classes) driving the DUT through Icarus — every class name is identical to SystemVerilog UVM.

DlaTest (uvm_test) — builds env, starts sequence, checks tally
DlaEnv (uvm_env) — wires analysis ports
DlaAgent (uvm_agent)
├ Sequencer — routes DlaOp items
├ Driver — the only pin‑wiggler
└ Monitor — passive; rebuilds C from pins
DlaScoreboard
golden matmul + checker
Sequence → Sequencer → Driver →(pins)→ DUT
DUT →(pins)→ Monitor →(observed C)→ Scoreboard
Driver →(applied A,B)──────────────→ Scoreboard

Mapped to the accelerator

  • DlaOp = one matmul job (A 4×256 weights, B 256×4 inputs).
  • Sequence = 1 directed (A=B=1 ⇒ every C=256) + 3 constrained‑random ops.
  • Driver = real protocol: stream A/B, pulse start, wait wb_done, read 16 C.
  • Monitor = reconstructs the 16 C outputs from the read‑back bus.
  • Scoreboard = predicts C=A·B (INT8, 24‑bit wrap) and compares.

[directed_ones] PASS: 16/16 match (C[0][0]=256)
[rand_0] PASS  [rand_1] PASS  [rand_2] PASS
ALL 4 TRANSACTIONS PASSED — 4 passed, 0 failed

10

Decisions & reproducing the views

Notes for the reviewer

Why C moved to flip‑flops

C holds only 16 accumulators (48 bytes) — a wasteful 64×8 macro. As flip‑flops it costs ~408 registers (tiny in an 85k‑instance die), removes a macro, cuts writeback 48→16 cycles, and drops the C read latency 4–5→1 cycle. A/B stay SRAM because they need four parallel 8‑bit lanes each.

Why cluster the macros

A roomy die spreads the memories apart, so the SRAM→PE broadcast nets route long and trip antennas. Pulling the 8 macros into a compact central block (55 µm channels) shortens those nets at the source; a density sweep then finds the placement (d50) that routes the residue clean. Result: antenna 0, timing/DRC/LVS unchanged.
